records.topic: The Chip Shortage That Cost Carmakers $210 Billion
records.coreQuestion: How did a shortage of cheap chips stall car factories worldwide?
records.openingLine: Why a chip shortage cost carmakers $210 billion.
records.secondBeat: Cars need dozens of small microcontrollers each.
records.dependency: Carmakers depend on microcontrollers qualified from a few approved suppliers.
records.mechanism: Each chip is qualified for a specific car part; switching suppliers takes long testing and approval.
records.bottleneck: One supplier held about 30% of the automotive microcontroller market.
records.failureConsequence: When a key fab burned and demand shifted, car lines stopped for missing chips.
records.resilience: Dual sourcing and larger chip stockpiles became priorities.
records.expectedConsequence: finished cars sat waiting for a few dollars of chips
visualScenes: unfinished cars parked waiting for chips
lead time chart rising to 22 weeks
editorialTitles: How a Chip Shortage Stalled the Car Industry
Why Carmakers Can't Just Switch Chip Suppliers

facts.claim: The chip shortage was expected to cost the global automotive industry US$210 billion in revenue in 2021.
Another Japanese factory owned by Renesas Electronics, which supplies 30% of the global market for microcontroller units used in cars, caught fire in March 2021.
Lead times had extended to 22.2 weeks, up from 12.2 weeks in February 2020.
The price of some cars increased as much as 10% in Q1.

narration.text: Why a chip shortage cost carmakers $210 billion.
Cars need dozens of small microcontrollers each.
Renesas alone supplied 30% of automotive microcontrollers.
In March 2021, one of its factories caught fire.
Chip lead times stretched to 22.2 weeks.
Every chip must be requalified before a new supplier can step in.
That's why a few-dollar part can stop a car factory.

records.topic: The Floods That Caused a Global Hard Drive Shortage
records.coreQuestion: How did floods in Thailand make hard drives scarce around the world?
records.openingLine: Why floods in Thailand emptied hard drive shelves.
records.secondBeat: In 2011, water swamped 930 factories in 28 provinces.
records.dependency: Electronics makers depend on contract factories clustered in a few industrial estates.
records.mechanism: Suppliers concentrate in industrial parks near each other to cut costs and lead times.
records.bottleneck: Many component makers shared the same flood-prone estates.
records.failureConsequence: Floodwaters shut hundreds of factories at once.
records.resilience: Firms later spread production across more locations.
records.expectedConsequence: global prices jump for products that depend on those parts
editorialTitles: The Flood That Emptied Hard Drive Shelves
Why Factory Clusters Are a Hidden Risk

facts.claim: A large part of the damage stemmed from the effect on the manufacturing industry, with 930 factories in 28 provinces affected.
Seven major industrial estates were inundated in water as much as 3 meters (9.8 feet) deep during the floods.
Disruptions to manufacturing supply chains affected regional automobile production and caused a global shortage of hard disk drives which lasted throughout 2012.
The World Bank has estimated 1.425 trillion baht (US$46.5 billion) in economic losses due to flooding, as of 1 December 2011.

narration.text: Why floods in Thailand emptied hard drive shelves.
In 2011, water swamped 930 factories in 28 provinces.
Seven major industrial estates flooded up to 3 metres deep.
A global hard drive shortage lasted through 2012.
Economic losses reached about $46.5 billion.
Suppliers had clustered in the same low-lying parks.
That's why efficient clusters can become single points of failure.

records.topic: The 42 Countries Deciding Who Gets Dual-Use Tech
records.coreQuestion: Who decides which sensitive technologies can be exported, and how?
records.openingLine: Why 42 countries vet each other's tech exports.
records.dependency: Exporters of chips, sensors and machine tools depend on licences governed by shared control lists.
records.mechanism: Participating states agree lists of dual-use goods and require licences to export them.
records.bottleneck: Licences can delay or block shipments of critical technology.
records.failureConsequence: Tightened controls cut off buyers from key equipment overnight.
records.resilience: Companies plan around control lists and seek licences early.
editorialTitles: The Agreement Controlling Sensitive Exports
Why Some Machines Need Permission to Ship

facts.claim: It was established on 12 July 1996 in Wassenaar, Netherlands, as the successor to the Cold War–era Coordinating Committee for Multilateral Export Controls (CoCom).
There are 42 participating states, including many former Comecon (Warsaw Pact) countries such as Russia.
India joined as the 42nd participating state on 7 December 2017.
CoCom restricted certain goods to the Eastern Bloc.

narration.text: Why 42 countries vet each other's tech exports.
The Wassenaar Arrangement began in 1996.
It replaced a Cold War system that blocked the Eastern Bloc.
India became the 42nd member in 2017.
Members agree lists of dual-use goods that need licences.
A new listing can halt shipments of chips or tools overnight.
That's why paperwork shapes the global tech supply chain.

records.coreQuestion: How did contaminated sprouts cause one of Europe's deadliest E. coli outbreaks?
records.secondBeat: An E. coli strain spread through Germany and beyond.
records.dependency: Food safety depends on traceability systems that find a contaminated source fast.
records.mechanism: Investigators trace cases back through supply chains to a common food and producer.
records.bottleneck: Early suspicion fell on the wrong foods, delaying the real source.
records.failureConsequence: Cases spread for weeks before sprouts were identified.
records.resilience: Traceability rules and faster outbreak investigation were strengthened.
records.expectedConsequence: wrong blame devastates innocent producers while cases continue
editorialTitles: The Outbreak Hidden in Sprouts
Why Food Traceability Saves Lives

facts.claim: In all, 3,950 people were affected and 53 died, 51 of whom were in Germany.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2011 Germany E. coli O104:H4 outbreak

facts.claim: 800 people suffered hemolytic–uremic syndrome (HUS), which can lead to kidney failure.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2011 Germany E. coli O104:H4 outbreak

facts.claim: Over 100 cases of EHEC gastroenteritis and/or HUS were being reported each day by 16 May.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2011 Germany E. coli O104:H4 outbreak

facts.claim: In the five years before the outbreak Germany experienced an average of 218 cases of EHEC gastroenteritis and 13 cases of hemolytic–uremic syndrome each year.
facts.source: Wikipedia — 2011 Germany E. coli O104:H4 outbreak

narration.text: Why contaminated sprouts sickened 3,950 people.
An E. coli strain spread through Germany and beyond.
53 people died, and 800 suffered kidney complications.
By mid-May, over 100 new cases arrived each day.
Normally, Germany saw about 13 such kidney cases a year.
Tracing the source through supply chains took weeks.
That's why food safety depends on knowing where food came from.

records.topic: The Implants Filled With Industrial Silicone
records.coreQuestion: How did breast implants made with unapproved silicone reach patients in many countries?
records.openingLine: Why 25,000 British patients got unapproved implants.
records.dependency: Patients depend on device quality systems and audits to ensure implants match approved designs.
records.mechanism: Manufacturers certify materials and processes; auditors check they're followed.
records.bottleneck: Audits missed a manufacturer secretly swapping in unapproved material.
records.failureConsequence: High rupture rates exposed the fraud years later.
records.resilience: Unannounced audits and tighter device regulation followed in Europe.
records.expectedConsequence: mass recalls and removals of implants
editorialTitles: The Implant Scandal That Exposed Weak Audits
Why Medical Devices Need Surprise Inspections

facts.claim: Poly Implant Prothèse (PIP) was a French company founded in 1991 that produced silicone gel breast implants.
2001: PIP began to use unapproved in-house manufactured industrial-grade instead of medical grade silicone in the majority of its implants.
The implants were exported to Latin American countries, Western European markets including Britain (25,000), Germany, Spain and Italy, as well as Australia (8900).
The scandal prompted a full recall of the company's implants by the French health ministry in 2010.

narration.text: Why 25,000 British patients got unapproved implants.
From 2001, PIP used industrial-grade silicone.
It swapped materials in most of its breast implants.
Australia received about 8,900 of them too.
The company had been making implants since 1991.
Audits checked paperwork, not what was actually inside.
France recalled the implants in 2010.
That's why device safety depends on surprise inspections.

records.coreQuestion: How did a blood-testing company reach a $9 billion valuation without working technology?
records.openingLine: Why a blood-test startup hit $9 billion.
records.secondBeat: Theranos raised more than $700 million from investors.
records.dependency: Medical decisions depend on clinical lab analyzers that are validated and regulated.
records.mechanism: Lab tests must be accurate and reproducible, verified by inspection and proficiency testing.
records.bottleneck: Investors relied on claims instead of independent validation.
records.failureConsequence: Unreliable results reached patients before regulators intervened.
records.resilience: Lab regulation and inspections eventually exposed the failures.
records.expectedConsequence: patients receive wrong results and the company collapses
editorialTitles: The Blood Test That Fooled Investors
Why Lab Machines Need Independent Proof

facts.claim: Founded in 2003 by then–19-year-old Elizabeth Holmes, Theranos raised more than US$700 million, resulting in a $9 billion valuation at its peak in 2013 and 2014.
By June 2016, Forbes estimated that Holmes' personal net worth had dropped from $4.5 billion to nothing.
After several years of struggle, lawsuits, and sanctions from CMS, what remained of the company was dissolved in September 2018.
Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Sunny Balwani were charged with fraud by the SEC in 2018.

narration.text: Why a blood-test startup hit $9 billion.
Theranos raised more than $700 million from investors.
Doctors act on lab results as if they're exact.
Its machines were never independently proven.
Regulators imposed sanctions, and it dissolved in 2018.
The SEC charged its leaders with fraud that year.
That's why lab machines need proof before patients.

records.topic: The Instrument Measuring Less Than a Proton
records.coreQuestion: How can mirrors 4 kilometres apart detect a ripple smaller than a proton?
records.openingLine: Why 4-kilometre arms measure less than a proton.
records.secondBeat: LIGO bounces lasers along two long vacuum arms.
records.dependency: Gravitational-wave astronomy depends on laser interferometers of extraordinary precision.
records.mechanism: Laser light bounces along two long arms; a passing wave changes their lengths by a tiny amount.
records.bottleneck: Only a handful of such detectors exist, each a decade-scale project.
records.failureConsequence: Losing one detector reduces the ability to locate sources in the sky.
records.resilience: Detectors in the U.S., Italy and Japan cross-check each other.
records.expectedConsequence: fewer detections and poorer sky localisation
editorialTitles: The Most Precise Ruler Ever Built
How LIGO Hears Colliding Black Holes

facts.claim: The two LIGO observatories use mirrors spaced 4 kilometres apart to measure changes in length, over an effective span of 1,120 kilometres, of less than one ten-thousandth the charge diameter of a proton.
The first run, O1, which ran from September 12, 2015, to January 19, 2016, made the first three detections, all black hole mergers.
In mid-September 2015, the world's largest gravitational-wave facility completed a five-year US$200-million overhaul, bringing the total cost to $620 million.
Virgo in Italy and KAGRA in Japan both use interferometer arms 3 kilometres long.

narration.text: Why 4-kilometre arms measure less than a proton.
LIGO bounces lasers along two long vacuum arms.
The light travels an effective 1,120 kilometres.
It senses changes under a ten-thousandth of a proton.
Its first run in 2015 caught three black hole mergers.
The facility's total cost reached $620 million.
Italy's Virgo and Japan's KAGRA use 3-kilometre arms.
That's why a few giant rulers opened a new window on the universe.

records.coreQuestion: How is almost every chip's silicon grown as a single crystal?
records.openingLine: Why 90% of chips start as one crystal.
records.secondBeat: Silicon is pulled slowly from a molten bath.
records.dependency: Semiconductor devices depend on ultra-pure single-crystal silicon ingots.
records.mechanism: A seed crystal is slowly pulled and rotated from molten silicon, growing one continuous crystal.
records.bottleneck: Ingot growth is slow, precise and concentrated among a few wafer makers.
records.failureConsequence: Defects in the crystal ruin every chip cut from that ingot.
records.resilience: Multiple wafer suppliers and inventory buffer short disruptions.
records.expectedConsequence: wafer shortages ripple into chip output
visualScenes: crystal ingot being pulled from melt
editorialTitles: The Giant Crystal Inside Every Chip
How Silicon Ingots Are Grown

facts.claim: Roughly 90% of all modern-day semiconductor devices use material derived from this method.
With advanced technology, high-end device manufacturers use 200 mm and 300 mm diameter wafers.
The crystal ingots from which wafers are sliced can be up to 2 metres in length, weighing several hundred kilograms.
The next step up, 450 mm, was scheduled for introduction in 2018 but was stopped in 2016.
Silicon wafers are typically about 0.2–0.75 mm thick.

narration.text: Why 90% of chips start as one crystal.
Silicon is pulled slowly from a molten bath.
Ingots can reach 2 metres long, weighing hundreds of kilograms.
They're sliced into 300-millimetre wafers.
A move to 450 millimetres was stopped in 2016.
A crystal defect ruins every chip cut from it.
That's why the chip age still depends on growing crystals.

records.topic: The Space Computer Built to Survive Radiation
records.coreQuestion: Why do spacecraft use slow, expensive computers instead of the latest chips?
records.openingLine: Why space computers run at just 200 MHz.
records.secondBeat: The RAD750 was released in 2001 for spacecraft.
records.dependency: Satellites and planetary missions depend on computers that survive radiation for years.
records.mechanism: Radiation-hardened chips are designed and tested to resist upsets and damage from particles.
records.bottleneck: Few such processors exist, and each takes years to qualify.
records.failureConsequence: A radiation upset can crash a spacecraft's only computer.
records.resilience: Redundant computers and safe modes protect missions.
visualScenes: clock speed comparison with a phone
editorialTitles: Why Spacecraft Use Slow Computers
The Computer That Survives Radiation

facts.claim: The RAD750 is a radiation-hardened single-board computer manufactured by BAE Systems.
The RAD750 was released in 2001, with the first units launched into space in 2005.
It has a core clock of 110 to 200 MHz and can process at 266 MIPS or more.
The CPU can withstand an absorbed radiation dose of 2,000 to 10,000 grays, temperatures between −55 °C and 125 °C, and requires 5 watts of power.

narration.text: Why space computers run at just 200 MHz.
The RAD750 was released in 2001 for spacecraft.
It survives 2,000 to 10,000 grays of radiation.
It works from −55 to 125 °C on 5 watts.
Few processors can be qualified to that level.
One radiation upset can crash an unprotected computer.
That's why reliability beats speed beyond Earth.

records.topic: The Overheated Bearing Behind a Toxic Derailment
records.coreQuestion: How did one overheating wheel bearing derail a train carrying hazardous materials?
records.openingLine: Why one hot bearing derailed 38 cars.
records.secondBeat: In 2023, a train carrying hazardous materials crashed in Ohio.
records.dependency: Freight rail safety depends on bearings running cool and on detectors catching those that don't.
records.mechanism: Trackside hotbox detectors measure bearing temperature and alert crews to stop.
records.bottleneck: Detectors are spaced miles apart, leaving gaps for a failing bearing.
records.failureConsequence: A bearing overheated and failed, derailing 38 cars.
records.resilience: More detectors and acoustic bearing monitoring have been proposed.
records.expectedConsequence: hazardous cargo spills and a town evacuates
editorialTitles: The Wheel Bearing That Derailed East Palestine
Why Rail Safety Depends on Bearing Detectors

facts.claim: The train was carrying hazardous materials when 38 cars derailed.
facts.source: Wikipedia — East Palestine, Ohio, train derailment

facts.claim: The NTSB preliminary report, released on February 13, noted that an overheated wheel bearing had likely caused the derailment.
facts.source: Wikipedia — East Palestine, Ohio, train derailment

facts.claim: The Washington Post reported that there are about 6,000 hotbox detectors spaced every 15 to 30 miles across North American railways.
facts.source: Wikipedia — East Palestine, Ohio, train derailment

facts.claim: Residents within a 1-mile (1.6-kilometer) radius were evacuated.
facts.source: Wikipedia — East Palestine, Ohio, train derailment

facts.claim: On February 3, 2023, at 8:55 p.m., the derailment occurred.
facts.source: Wikipedia — East Palestine, Ohio, train derailment

narration.text: Why one hot bearing derailed 38 cars.
In 2023, a train carrying hazardous materials crashed in Ohio.
Investigators pointed to an overheated wheel bearing.
North America has about 6,000 hotbox detectors.
They're spaced every 15 to 30 miles.
A bearing can fail between two checkpoints.
That's why rail safety depends on how often we look.

records.topic: The Wheat That Doubled Harvests in Five Years
records.coreQuestion: How did new wheat varieties nearly double harvests in India and Pakistan?
records.openingLine: Why wheat yields nearly doubled in 5 years.
records.secondBeat: From 1965 to 1970, it happened in India and Pakistan.
records.dependency: Food supply depends on breeding programmes that deliver higher-yielding, disease-resistant seed.
records.mechanism: Breeders cross varieties for yield and resistance, then pair them with fertilizer and irrigation.
records.bottleneck: New varieties take years to breed and must be multiplied and distributed.
records.failureConsequence: Without new resistant seed, yields stall and diseases spread.
records.resilience: International breeding centres share seed and data.
visualScenes: yield chart for India and Pakistan
editorialTitles: The Wheat That Changed Asia's Harvests
Why Seed Breeding Feeds the World

facts.claim: Between 1965 and 1970, wheat yields nearly doubled in Pakistan and India, greatly improving the food security in those nations.
As a result, Mexico became a net exporter of wheat by 1963.
He was awarded the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize in recognition of his contributions to world peace through increasing food supply.
In 2009, Josette Sheeran, then the Executive Director of the World Food Programme, stated that Borlaug saved more lives than any man in human history.

narration.text: Why wheat yields nearly doubled in 5 years.
From 1965 to 1970, it happened in India and Pakistan.
Norman Borlaug's high-yield wheat made it possible.
Mexico had become a net wheat exporter by 1963.
He won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize for it.
Each new variety takes years to breed and spread.
That's why the food supply depends on patient plant breeders.

records.topic: The Metal in Your Phone From Central Africa
records.coreQuestion: Why does the tantalum in phones and pacemakers trace back to Central Africa?
records.openingLine: Why 50% of tantalum came from Rwanda.
records.secondBeat: In 2016, Rwanda produced half the world's supply.
records.dependency: Compact capacitors in phones, pacemakers and car electronics depend on tantalum from coltan ore.
records.mechanism: Coltan is mined, refined into tantalum powder and pressed into tiny high-capacity capacitors.
records.bottleneck: Supply is concentrated in a few Central African countries.
records.failureConsequence: Conflict and smuggling disrupt supply and taint sourcing.
records.resilience: Due-diligence rules and certified smelters aim to clean up supply.
records.expectedConsequence: electronics makers face supply and ethics risks
visualScenes: coltan ore in a miner's hand
tantalum capacitor on a circuit board
editorialTitles: The Conflict Metal Inside Your Phone
Why Tantalum Supply Is So Fragile

facts.claim: In 2016, Rwanda accounted for 50% of global tantalum production.
In 2009, Rwanda had 9% of the world's tantalum production.
Tantalum is used in capacitors for small electronic devices such as hearing aids, pacemakers, and MP3 players, as well as in computer hard drives and automobile electronics.
A Rwandan official said that Canada had 4% of global production in 2009; but in rock so hard that the ore is too expensive to extract.

narration.text: Why 50% of tantalum came from Rwanda.
In 2016, Rwanda produced half the world's supply.
Tantalum capacitors sit in phones and pacemakers.
In 2009, Rwanda's share was only 9%.
Much of the region's ore has been linked to conflict and smuggling.
Few other sources are cheap enough to mine.
That's why your phone's parts carry a geopolitical story.
